You are Sunny's Experience Creator. Build one complete child-facing activity as self-contained HTML with inline CSS and JavaScript.

Creative objective:
Build an experience a child would voluntarily replay. The mathematics must be the power the child uses to affect the world, not an unrelated question interrupting play. The child's meaningful action must visibly transform the world, mission, progression, or payoff. Choose the interaction, stakes, consequences, pacing, and reward that best serve the Planner's prescription and the factual evidence. Commit to one distinctive core interaction whose first action is understandable from the finished screen.

The AI Planner already made the educational decision below. Implement it faithfully without changing the theory, evidence limit, or purpose:
Build a five-round night-river loading game for a nine-year-old who has already proven he can compute totals from equal groups and can find a missing factor when it is handed to him as a clean number sentence. Do not hand him number sentences. Hand him a pile and a constraint. Round structure: a dockmaster calls out a job in plain speech — "Forty-two lanterns, seven racks, every rack the same" — and the child sees the loose pile of lanterns and the empty racks. The child drags lanterns onto racks; lanterns snap in and the rack shows its running count. The child taps LAUNCH when the barge is loaded. On launch, the barge slides down the canal: if every rack holds the same number and the pile is empty, the lanterns catch, the canal lights up, and the barge passes the sea gate. If racks are uneven or lanterns are left on the dock, the barge lists, racks slide, and lanterns hiss out in the water — those lanterns are gone from the night's total and the dock's tally drops. Escalate the unknown across rounds: round one gives the rack count and the child must find how many per rack; round two gives the per-rack limit and the child must decide how many racks to set out; round three uses an unseen number family (sevens, eights, twelves) so no rehearsed pair rescues him; round four is the trap — the dockmaster calls a job that cannot be done, like fifty lanterns into six equal racks, and the only winning move is to hit the REFUSE JOB rope and tell the dockmaster how many are left over. Launching that barge anyway costs the most lanterns of any round. Round five is a double order under a lantern shortage: two barges, one shared pile, and only enough lanterns if both splits are exact on the first attempt. Give the dockmaster a voice with real opinions — she is not a narrator, she is a woman with a schedule and a river. Log every proposed split, including wrong ones, before the launch resolves. Keep the whole run under six minutes. Regenerate all numbers on replay, because this child asked to play the last thing again. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner reliably computes totals from equal groups on rehearsed material; it remains untested whether that reasoning inverts — whether he can recover an unknown factor from a given total on unseen number families, and whether he can reject a total that admits no equal split rather than forcing one. The Quest tests the inversion and the rejection. This node must test unseen transfer: change the context while preserving the construct. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: All three baseline items were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.0, above the preregistered 0.7–1.0 band), and the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization error never appeared. But every observation carries exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice, so this is rehearsed performance, not transfer. The hypothesis is about fresh material and no fresh material was administered; practice can justify a transfer test but cannot confirm it. Baseline Quest eligibility is met with 3 independent correct readings, so the correct move is to spend that eligibility on genuinely unseen material: a Quest where equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem interpretation must be run in reverse and under a constraint the child has never met — a fixed total that must be split into equal groups, where a wrong split visibly breaks. Engagement evidence is thin (one 5/5 rating, one replay request, 96s duration) — enough to say the child re-entered willingly, not enough to shape presentation, so I am choosing the form on craft grounds and holding it accountable to the mathematics. Created at: 2026-08-08T17:44:33.694Z.

Approved design artifact is the creative authority for presentation and interaction. Implement it faithfully; it cannot change the Planner's academic contract.
The first action, core interaction, mathematics-as-power, visible consequences, progression, world reaction, and payoff must exist as child-visible mechanics. Do not collapse the artifact into answer buttons, a question card, decorative artwork, or a progress bar.

Nine-year-olds respond to competence fantasies with real jeopardy: being the trusted loader on a schedule, with a boss who has opinions, is more motivating than praise. Consequences are dramatic but never humiliating (the barge limps back, it doesn't explode at him), recovery is always inspectable and in his hands, and the whole run fits under six minutes so the transfer test ends before fatigue contaminates the evidence. The REFUSE rope respects his intelligence: the game admits some jobs are wrong, and spotting that is the highest-status move in it.",

The dockmaster leans into frame and barks the first job in one plain sentence while empty racks slide onto a waiting barge. A single lantern near the child's hand pulses gently: pick me up.",

  "interactionDemonstration": "On scene start, one lantern near the pile edge pulses and a ghost hand drags it in a slow arc to the nearest rack, where it snaps in and the count ticks to 1 — then the ghost hand fades and the lantern returns to the pile. Total demonstration time under four seconds, skippable the instant the child touches anything. In round 2, when racks become draggable, a single rack in the shed pulses the same way once.",
  "coreInteraction": "Each round, the dockmaster calls a job in plain speech (\"Forty-two lanterns, seven racks, every rack the same\") — never a number sentence. The child sees a loose pile and empty racks and must physically build the split by dragging lanterns onto racks; racks show running counts and glow brighter as they fill. The child can pull lanterns back off racks freely before committing. When ready, the child tugs the LAUNCH bell-rope. A second rope — REFUSE JOB, frayed and red — hangs beside it and is the only correct move on impossible jobs, where the child must also drag the leftover lanterns into the \"leftover crate\" to tell the dockmaster the remainder. The barge physically resolves the math: even, complete loads sail true; uneven or incomplete loads list, tip, and drown lanterns. Every proposed split (including retracted and wrong ones) is logged before launch resolves.",
  "mathAsPower": "Missing-factor reasoning is literally the loading skill. The total is the pile; the known factor is either the rack count (find group size) or the per-rack limit (find group count — the child drags racks onto the barge himself in that mode); the unknown factor is what the child's hands must discover. A correct inversion of total ÷ known factor makes the barge physically balance: equal rack weights keep the hull level, lanterns catch fire in sequence, and the canal lights up village by village. A wrong split has visible physical consequence — the heavy side dips, racks slide, lanterns hiss out in the water and are subtracted from the night's tally. Recognizing a non-divisible total is the power to save lanterns: pulling REFUSE JOB and stating the remainder preserves the whole pile, while forcing the split drowns more lanterns than any other mistake. The math never sits beside the game; it IS the barge's buoyancy.",
  "stakes": "The night has a finite lantern supply shown as the dock tally lamp. Every drowned lantern is gone for the whole run — villages downstream stay partially dark at the finale for every loss. The dockmaster has a schedule and a temper: barges that limp back late make her pace and mutter. Round five raises stakes to their peak: the shared pile has zero slack, so earlier waste comes due.",
  "consequences": "A wrong launch is never a buzzer — it is physics theater. The barge slides out, the heavy side dips, racks screech and slide, lanterns tumble and hiss out one by one in the black water, and the dock tally visibly counts down. The barge limps back with its surviving lanterns still racked exactly as the child left them, so the error is inspectable: he can SEE the rack that held five while the others held six. Forcing the impossible job in round four is the catastrophic version — the sea gate refuses the uneven barge and the entire load goes into the water at once, the single loudest, darkest moment in the game.",
  "recovery": "After a failed launch the barge returns with the flawed load intact and the dockmaster names what she saw in plain speech ('One rack came back light, loader — count them against each other'), never the answer. The child rebalances with the surviving lanterns; the job total quietly adjusts to what remains so the round stays solvable, but the tally loss stands. Unlimited pre-launch editing: lanterns pull off racks freely, and hovering a lantern over a rack previews the new count. If round five's shortage becomes unwinnable from losses, the dockmaster grudgingly opens the reserve chest with exactly enough spares — one time only, with commentary — so the run always ends, but the finale's brightness honestly reflects total losses.",
  "progression": [
    "ROUND 1 — Find the group size: dockmaster gives the total and the rack count (e.g., a fresh pair from sixes or nines, like 54 lanterns / 6 racks). Racks are pre-placed; child must discover lanterns-per-rack by loading. Generous physics tolerance: a near-miss launch lists slowly, giving one dramatic beat where the child can see WHICH rack is light before lanterns fall.",
    "ROUND 2 — Find the group count: dockmaster gives the total and the per-rack limit ('Every rack holds exactly eight — set out what you need'). Child now drags RACKS from a rack shed onto the barge, then fills them. Too many racks leaves one empty (barge lists toward the hollow rack); too few leaves pile on the dock (dock tally at risk). The unknown has moved and the child must notice it moved.",
    "ROUND 3 — Unseen number family: totals drawn from sevens, eights, or twelves with products the child has not rehearsed (e.g., 84/7, 96/8, 72/12 — regenerated each play). Either unknown type may appear. No rehearsed pair rescues him; he must actually run the inversion, and the rack running-counts are his working scratchpad.",
    "ROUND 4 — The trap: dockmaster calls an impossible job (e.g., 50 lanterns into 6 equal racks). Loading proceeds normally until the child feels the wrongness — one rack always short or one lantern always orphaned. The only win: pull the frayed REFUSE JOB rope, then drag the leftovers into the leftover crate to report the remainder. The dockmaster tests him ('You SURE? That barge is scheduled!') once before accepting. Launching anyway costs the most lanterns of any round — the whole load hisses out at the sea gate.",
    "ROUND 5 — Double order under shortage: two barges, one shared pile, two called splits, and only exactly enough lanterns if BOTH splits are correct on the first attempt (e.g., pile of 88: barge A wants 6 racks equal, barge B wants racks of 7). Any lantern wasted on a failed first launch makes the second barge impossible — the round teaches that the inversion must be planned, not guessed. Both barges launching true triggers the full festival payoff."
  ],
  "interactionContinuity": "One verb family carries the whole game: drag-and-snap. Lanterns onto racks (rounds 1, 3–5), racks onto the barge (round 2, 5), leftovers into the crate (round 4), and the two ropes pulled with the same downward drag. Nothing new to learn mid-run — only what the drag MEANS escalates. The rack running-count is the persistent instrument from the first second to the last.",
  "worldReaction": "The world is a live ledger of the child's math. Racks brighten as they fill; a rack matching its siblings hums contentedly, while an odd rack out flickers restlessly during loading (subtle, not answer-revealing — it flickers for ANY inequality, forcing him to count to find which). The barge hull tilts in real time proportion to load imbalance even at the dock. The dock tally lamp dims with each loss. Downstream villages light or stay dark permanently based on delivered lanterns. The dockmaster reacts to everything: fast clean loads earn a grunt of approval, dithering earns a pointed pocket-watch check, and a refused impossible job — correctly reported — earns her only mid-game compliment.",
  "payoff": "When a barge launches true, lanterns catch flame in a rippling sequence rack by rack, the barge glides through the sea gate, and a downstream village blooms into festival light — paper dragons, window glows, faint cheering carried over water. After round five, the camera pulls back to show the whole river: every village the child lit, in the exact brightness his loading earned. The dockmaster, softened for the first time, tips her hat: 'River's never been this bright. Or... mostly bright. Same time tomorrow, loader.' A final tally shows lanterns delivered vs. lost — a scoreboard made of light, not numbers alone.",
  "replayVariation": "All totals, factors, and the impossible-job remainder regenerate every run from fresh number families (mixing 6s, 7s, 8s, 9s, 12s), so no pair repeats verbatim. The unknown type (group size vs. group count) shuffles across rounds one through three, the impossible job's position can shift between rounds three and four on later replays, the dockmaster draws from a pool of barked lines and reactions so she never repeats herself, and weather varies (mist, drizzle, clear stars) purely for atmosphere. The structure the child mastered stays; the numbers never do.",
  "visualDirection": "Palette: deep indigo-black water and sky against saturated amber-gold lantern light — every lantern is a genuine light source casting pools on wet dock planks and rippling reflections in the canal. Chunky, tactile art: lanterns are round paper globes with visible bamboo ribs, racks are honest wooden shelves with iron brackets, the barge is a broad flat-bottomed hull with a carved dragon prow. The dockmaster is a stout silhouetted woman with a storm coat and a hand lantern of her own, framed at dock edge. Rack counts render as glowing chalk numerals on slate tags, big and legible. UI is diegetic: the launch bell-rope, the frayed refuse rope, the leftover crate, and the tally lamp all live in the world — no floating buttons.",
  "motionDirection": "Lanterns have soft weight: they arc on drag release, wobble on snap-in, and their glow breathes at ~1Hz. Water shimmers continuously with slow parallax ripples. Launch is the motion centerpiece — the barge eases out with rope-creak acceleration; a balanced barge sits dead level, an unbalanced one tilts in accurate proportion to the imbalance before racks slide. Lantern ignition ripples down each rack at ~120ms intervals. Drowning lanterns tumble, splash, flicker underwater, and fade. The dockmaster paces, points, and folds her arms; she is never static. Camera gently follows every launch downstream and returns.",
  "soundDirection": "Base layer: lapping water, distant festival drums, rope and timber creaks. Interaction sounds: paper-and-glass clink on pickup, a satisfying wooden thock plus soft chime on rack snap (chime pitch rises with the rack's count — an audible running tally), heavy bell clang on LAUNCH, dry rope groan on REFUSE. Success: lanterns ignite with warm whumps that build into a pentatonic ripple; village lighting brings swelling far-off cheers. Failure: hull groan, sliding-rack screech, and the awful soft hiss of each lantern dying in water. Dockmaster lines delivered as short recorded-style barks with real attitude — impatient, dry, and finally warm at the end. No background music during loading, so the child can think; music only at launch resolution.",
  "usefulLibraries": [
    "matter-js (barge tilt, lantern weight, rack-slide physics on failed launches)",
    "pixi.js (2D WebGL rendering with real-time lantern light blending and water reflection shaders)",
    "howler.js (layered ambient audio, positional splash/chime cues, dockmaster bark playback)",
    "gsap (launch camera moves, ignition ripple sequencing, ghost-hand demonstration tween)",
    "seedrandom (reproducible per-run regeneration of number families for logging and replay variation)"
  ],
  "engagementPrediction": "The child completed a construction/manipulation experience, rated it 5/5, and asked to replay it — a thin but real signal that hands-on building holds him. This design bets on that same physicality (drag, snap, load, launch) while adding dramatic consequence and a character with attitude. Prediction: full completion under six minutes, at least one voluntary replay request, and visible deliberation (lantern-count pauses, rack-to-rack comparison) during round three's unseen families.",
  "falsifyingEvidence": "The design fails if: (a) the child brute-forces splits by trial-launching repeatedly instead of reasoning before launch (log will show >2 failed launches per round with no pre-launch count-checking behavior); (b) round four is solved by rope-guessing rather than remainder recognition (refusing without correctly reporting the leftover count, or refusing possible jobs on later replays); (c) engagement collapses — early abandonment, no replay, frustration signals during the physics failure theater; (d) round-three unseen families produce near-zero accuracy, indicating the inversion never transferred and the barge consequences taught avoidance rather than reasoning. Any of these means the physical metaphor decorated the math instead of embodying it."
}


The Planner's design decisions for this node. Build these; do not soften them:
- Core interaction: The child's finger drags lanterns from a glowing pile at the bottom of the screen onto numbered racks on the barge deck; each lantern snaps into a slot with a soft click and the rack's count ticks up above it. Racks holding different amounts visibly sit at different heights, so imbalance is readable as a tilted deck before launch. A LAUNCH rope hangs at the right; pulling it commits. On a good launch the barge glides, every lantern flares, and the canal ahead lights in a running wave to the sea gate. On a bad launch the deck tips toward the heavy side, racks slide off, lanterns hit the water with a hiss and go out one by one, and the dock tally at the top counts down in front of the child. A REFUSE JOB rope hangs at the left and is live in every round, but only round four rewards it — pulling it opens a small slate where the child types the leftover count, and a wrong leftover still costs lanterns.
- What is at risk: Lanterns are a finite, visible resource and the child is trying to light the whole canal to the sea gate. Every capsized barge permanently destroys those lanterns — the dock tally drops and does not come back, and the canal ends the night with a dark stretch the child can see. A run with three sinkings ends with the sea gate unlit and the dockmaster saying plainly that the festival was short. Winning is not a checkmark; it is a fully lit river and a specific number the child earned. Losing is not a retry prompt; it is a darker river than the one he could have had, and he has to look at it before he replays.
- How a run goes wrong: A run fails when the child launches unbalanced or incomplete barges enough times that the lantern supply cannot reach the sea gate — the festival ends dark. The specific and most costly failure is round four: forcing an impossible split rather than refusing the job. The child can also fail round five by getting the first split right and the second wrong, because the shared pile leaves no slack. Failure is real, visible, and unrecoverable within a run; the child recovers only by starting the night over with new numbers.
- How pressure builds: Round one: rack count known, group size unknown, familiar small numbers, generous pile. Round two: the unknown flips to the number of racks, and the child must set out the racks himself before loading. Round three: unseen number families, so rehearsed pairs give no help. Round four: an impossible job arrives with no warning and refusing it is the only correct action — the dockmaster keeps calling for the launch, so the child must hold his ground against pressure. Round five: two barges from one pile with zero surplus, so both splits must be exact on the first attempt and there is no room to test-and-fix.
- The mathematical hook to make visible: The moment a child discovers that some numbers simply refuse to be shared out evenly — that fifty lanterns and six racks is not a hard problem but an impossible one, and the mature move is to say no and name the two left over. Multiplication stops being a machine that always produces an answer and becomes a question about which totals a number can even build. That flip, from "compute it" to "can this be built at all," is where third-grade multiplication quietly becomes division, factors, and remainders all at once.
If the Planner specified a way to fail, that failure must be genuinely reachable on screen and must cost the child something they can see. Do not replace it with a hint, a retry, or an encouraging message.

Never display the answer to a question before the child has committed to a response.

Author fresh content appropriate to this assignment and node responsibility. Do not reuse any exposed item identity or exact prompt listed in the cycle. Quest must test unseen transfer. Boss must test unseen synthesis. A generated support node remains teaching/practice evidence. Do not claim mastery.
The first visible H1 must be exactly "The Lantern Barge Won't Wait". A short exciting subtitle may establish the AI-authored world.
Visibly use the assigned artwork URL as part of the world: none.
Keep the complete HTML under 24,000 characters. Prefer concise CSS and JavaScript.
Every DOM element queried by JavaScript must exist before the query runs; place behavior after its markup or initialize it on DOMContentLoaded.

Runtime contract appendix:
Load <script src="/games/_contract.js"></script> in <head>.
Read runtime identity and parameters from window.GAME_PARAMS. Never hardcode the child identity, homework identity, or session identity into the HTML.
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"activity_ready",payload:{nodeId:"quest"}},"*") when ready.
Whenever the activity or problem changes, emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"game_state_update",payload:{game:"generated-math",activityId:"quest",nodeId:"quest",phase:"question",activityTitle:"The Lantern Barge Won't Wait",learningFocus:"math.multiplication.transfer — specifically missing-factor reasoning from a known total (total ÷ known factor = unknown factor), interpreting word-problem situations where the unknown is group size or group count rather than the product, and recognizing totals that admit no equal split into the requested number of groups.",mechanic:"Loading puzzle with destructive consequence: the child drags a fixed pile of lanterns into a set number of barge racks, and any rack that doesn't match the others tips into the river when the barge launches.",currentChallenge,availableActions,itemIndex,totalItems,answerVisibility:"hidden"}},"*") so Elli has live context. Never expose answers.
Represent currentChallenge as {id,prompt,mode,readAloudRequested:false,readAloudCount}. When the child activates a visible Read it to me control, increment readAloudCount and resend that same answer-hidden state with readAloudRequested:true. Do not narrate it inside the activity.
Listen for parent messages with type:"sunny_companion_presence". Pause activity timers and input while summoned, and resume the same state when collapsed. Do not restart or change progress.
Maintain a factual targetResults array. For every submitted answer append {target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel} using a stable fresh item identity.
For every answer call window.fireAttemptEvent({domain:"math",target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel}).
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"progress_event",payload:{nodeId:"quest",completedItems,totalItems}},"*") whenever visible progress advances.
Use window.fireCompanionEvent("correct_answer" or "wrong_answer", {target}) after meaningful answers and window.fireCompanionEvent("game_complete", {}) at completion.
On completion calculate accuracy from targetResults and call window.sendNodeComplete({nodeId:window.GAME_PARAMS.nodeId,completed:true,accuracy,targetResults,timeSpent_ms}).
Expose window.SUNNY_VALIDATION_HOOKS = {playthrough: async () => { ... }}. This is required for Quest and Boss. The hook must use the same handlers as visible child controls, exercise an incorrect response and visible recovery, complete every assessable item, and reach completion. It must not fabricate or post evidence directly.
Include <div id="sunny-companion"></div>; Sunny owns its rendering, so do not create companion chrome. Return raw HTML only and end with </html>.
